newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ's Clark reassures markets on Labour-led govt.
newsitem.headline: NZ's Clark reassures markets on Labour-led govt.

text.p: New Zealand Labour leader Helen Clark, portraying herself as prime minister-in-waiting, reassured financial markets on Tuesday that a Labour-led government would keep the economy on track.
Clark said in an interview she was confident Reserve Bank Governor Don Brash could live with a proposed Labour widening of the central bank's inflation target.

She said she would insist on Labour's Michael Cullen becoming finance minister in any government she led after Saturday's general election, and all but ruled out a formal coalition with the left-wing Alliance.
Financial markets appear comfortable with Cullen and are worried about the policies of the Alliance, including big rises in taxation and expenditure and major amendments to the Reserve Bank Act.

"What's important is that Labour is clearly in the driving seat of the new government, that I am the prime minister and that Dr Cullen is the minister of finance," Clark told Reuters Financial Television.
"I don't think there's the slightest prospect of the Alliance entering a coalition, but the role they will play will be well understood by those who follow north European politics," she added.
Under this system, Clark said, smaller parties gave informal support to minority governments by voting with them on key policy measures.
She said Alliance economic policies "clearly can't be implemented", and its proposed tax increases would punish middle-income families.

However, Clark has also said she sees scope to work with the Alliance in areas such as housing, health, education, and repeal of the Employment Contracts Act which sharply curbed the powers of trade unions.

Opinion polls suggest a trio of Labour, the Alliance and economic nationalist New Zealand First is well placed to end six years of conservative National Party government in the country's first election under a new proportional system.
Clark said it was undesirable for the New Zealand dollar, whose rise over the past two years has hurt exporters, to keep on rising so fast.

"I have never been an advocate of a low dollar. I think that in the end a strong dollar is a good thing. But what has been difficult for exporters is the rapid rise in the dollar, and I don't think it's desirable that it keep rising so rapidly."
Clark, who pledges to share the fruits of economic recovery more widely, has run a strong campaign as she bids to be New Zealand's first woman prime minister.
A control group of floating voters rated Clark the winner of both major televised debates of the campaign, further boosting her cause in the closing days.
